e-477.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity
e-477.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad  \cos^2 x = 1-\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-478.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a $\tan^2{x}$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+\tan^2x =\sec^2x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
\tan^2 x =\sec^2 x -1.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \tan^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \left(\sec^2 x -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\tan x -x+C.	
	}
$$

e-479.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+\cot^2x =\csc^2 x.$ Rearranging this gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\cot^2 x &=\csc^2 x -1.
}
$$

Substituting this into our integral gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \left(5\cot^2 x -x^2\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \bigg(5\left(\csc^2 x -1 \right) -x^2\bigg) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\int \left(5\csc^2 x -5 -x^2\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=-5\cot x -5x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+C.	
	}
$$

e-480.knowledge_point: Integrating Trigonometric Expressions With Linear Arguments Using the Pythagorean Identities
e-480.worked_solution:
From the identity  $1+\tan^2 \theta =\sec^2 \theta$ with $\theta = 3x,$ we get 

$$
\eqalign{
		1+\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x)\
		\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x) -1.
}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\int 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x&= 2\int \tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x\
                                                                &= 2\int \left(\sec^2 (3x) -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
                                                                 &= 2\left(\int \sec^2 (3x)\, \textrm{d}x -\int1 \, \textrm{d}x\right)\
				                                &= 2\left( \dfrac{1}{3}\tan (3x) -x\right)+C\
                                                                 &= 	\dfrac{2}{3}\tan (3x) -2x+C.
	}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$
after.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡x=1-{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Calculate $\int 100{tan}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a ${tan}^{2}⁡x$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 100{tan}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int 100({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (100{sec}^{2}⁡x-100)\text{d}x \\  & =100\operatorname{tan}⁡x-100x+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a ${tan}^{2}⁡x$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{({tan}^{2}⁡x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
We use the cosecant-cotangent identity:

$$
1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =-0-(-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}

after.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{{cot}^{5}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$
after.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{cot}^{5}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{-\operatorname{cot}⁡x(1-{cot}^{4}⁡x)}{(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{-\operatorname{cot}⁡x(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)}{(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{-\operatorname{cot}⁡x{csc}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int -\operatorname{cot}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
From the identity  $1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =(5x+\pi ),$ we get 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi )={sec}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi ).
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (9{tan}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi )-5{x}^{4}+9)\,\text{d}x & =\int (9[1+{tan}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi )]-5{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (9{sec}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi )-5{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =9\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡(5x+\pi ))-5\cdot \frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C \\  & =\frac{9}{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡(5x+\pi )-{x}^{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Using 1+cot²(3x−2π)=csc²(3x−2π), the integrand becomes 4x³+7csc²(3x−2π). Integrating gives x⁴−(7/3)cot(3x−2π)+C, option e.

after.name: Question 19
after.worked_solution:
From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =3x-2\pi ,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{cot}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (7+4{x}^{3}+7{cot}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ))\,\text{d}x & =\int (4{x}^{3}+7+7{cot}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (4{x}^{3}+7[1+{cot}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi )])\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (4{x}^{3}+7{csc}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ))\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\cdot \frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+7(-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x-2\pi ))+C \\  & ={x}^{4}-\frac{7}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x-2\pi )+C.\end{aligned}
$$
